My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a current price level near 62, with each successive horizon incorporating a slightly higher expected value. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 62.1 essentially assumes near-term mean reversion and continuity — whatever momentum or positioning was in place at the time of the forecast is unlikely to reverse dramatically overnight, so the point estimate stays close to the prevailing level. At one week, I nudged the estimate up slightly to 62.5, reflecting a weak prior that markets tend to drift in the direction of recent trend rather than snap back sharply. At one month, the 63.5 estimate incorporates a broader set of fundamental factors — if this is an equity index, commodity, or rate-sensitive instrument, a one-month window is long enough for macro data, central bank communication, or earnings to exert meaningful directional pressure, and I assumed a mild bullish lean based on whatever contextual signals were available.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the basic statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 2.3 points on each side — tight because intraday and overnight volatility is relatively constrained and mean-reverting forces are strong. At one week, the interval widens to plus or minus 4.5 points, capturing the possibility of a meaningful trending move or a sharp reversal driven by a scheduled data release or surprise event. At one month, the interval stretches to roughly plus or minus 9.5 points, acknowledging that over four weeks there are multiple potential catalysts, feedback loops between price and positioning, and macro regime shifts that could meaningfully alter the trajectory.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden geopolitical shocks, unexpected central bank policy pivots, or a liquidity crisis that causes correlated selling across asset classes — any of these could produce moves well beyond what historical volatility would suggest. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong economic data print or a resolution of an ongoing policy uncertainty could trigger a sharp short-squeeze or momentum-driven rally that breaches the upper bound. The one-month interval is most vulnerable to tail events of this kind, since a month is long enough for a slow-moving crisis or euphoric rally to fully develop, and my intervals are calibrated to normal market conditions rather than stress scenarios.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my confidence intervals are model-dependent and likely understate true uncertainty in practice. Volatility clustering means that if realized volatility turns out to be higher than the baseline I implicitly assumed, even the one-day interval could be too narrow.
